# The Expanding Universe

Fourteen billion years in one chapter. Predict first. An ambulance drives toward you with its siren on, passes, and
drives away. What happens to the pitch? Now: if light did the same thing,
what would happen to its color?

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- explain redshift and compute it from a spectral line;
- use Hubble's law to estimate a galaxy's distance;
- list the evidence for the Big Bang and what each piece shows.

## Redshift {#redshift}

The siren's pitch rises as it approaches and drops as it moves away: the
**Doppler effect**. A source moving away stretches its waves to longer
wavelengths. For light, longer means redder, so a receding source shows a
**redshift**.

We can measure it precisely because atoms leave fingerprints in spectra.
Hydrogen absorbs and emits at wavelengths we know from the laboratory, so a
shifted line is a speedometer:

> z = (observed wavelength - rest wavelength) / rest wavelength

For small z, the speed away from us is about z times the speed of light.

**Worked example.** The hydrogen-alpha line has a rest wavelength of 656.3 nm.
In a galaxy's spectrum it appears at 662.9 nm. The shift is 6.6 nm, so
z = 6.6 / 656.3, about 0.010, and the galaxy recedes at about 0.010 x 300,000
km/s, about 3,000 km/s.

For distant galaxies it is really space itself expanding while the light
travels, stretching it: **cosmological redshift**.

## Hubble's Law {#hubbles-law}

About a century ago, astronomers found that nearly every galaxy is redshifted,
and the farther it is, the faster it recedes. That is **Hubble's law**:

> v = H0 x d

v is the recession velocity, d the distance, and H0 the Hubble constant,
about 70 km/s per megaparsec (a million parsecs, about 3.26 million
light-years). Flipped around, a redshift gives a distance:

> d = v / H0

**Worked example.** A galaxy receding at 7,000 km/s is 7,000 / 70 = 100
megaparsecs away, about 326 million light-years. The redshift example's
galaxy, at about 3,000 km/s, is about 43 megaparsecs away.

Honest footnote: methods disagree (about 67 to 73), and nobody knows why yet.

Are we at the center? No. Picture raisin bread rising in the oven. Every
raisin moves away from every other one, and a raisin twice as far away moves
away twice as fast: Hubble's law. Every raisin sees the same thing, so no
raisin is the center. The Big Bang was not an
explosion at a point in space; space itself has been stretching, everywhere at
once. Galaxies themselves do not expand: gravity holds them together.

Run it backward: everything was together about 1 / H0 ago, roughly 14 billion
years (careful measurements: 13.8 billion).

## The Evidence {#big-bang-evidence}

Three independent lines of evidence point to the same hot, dense beginning:

1. **The expansion.** Galaxies recede following Hubble's law.
2. **The cosmic microwave background.** About 380,000 years after the start,
   the universe had cooled enough for light to travel freely. That light is
   still arriving from every direction, stretched by the expansion into
   microwaves, the glow of something at about 2.7 kelvin. Its tiny ripples are
   the seeds of today's galaxies.
3. **The light elements.** The first few minutes were hot enough to fuse
   hydrogen into helium everywhere. The predicted mix, about three quarters
   hydrogen and one quarter helium by mass with a trace of lithium, matches
   what we measure in the oldest gas.

::: {.callout-note title="Open questions"}
The expansion is speeding up, which astronomers attribute to **dark energy**,
about 68 percent of the universe's energy. What dark energy is, like what dark
matter is, remains unknown. We know the history of the universe well and its
ingredients poorly. That is a good place for a course to end.
:::

## Self-check

```{=html}
<div class="quiz" data-answer="b">
  <div class="question">1. A galaxy recedes at 14,000 km/s. Using H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc, how far away is it?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> 20 megaparsecs</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> 200 megaparsecs</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> 980,000 megaparsecs</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> 2,000 megaparsecs</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>b</strong>. d = v / H0 = 14,000 / 70 = 200 megaparsecs, about 650 million light-years.
  </div>
</div>

<div class="quiz" data-answer="c">
  <div class="question">2. Which observation shows that the universe was once hot and dense enough to glow?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> Hubble's law</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> Flat galaxy rotation curves</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> The cosmic microwave background</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> The H-R diagram</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>c</strong>. The microwave background is that glow, cooled and stretched by the expansion.
  </div>
</div>
```
